question: us-policy-positions:transportation-infrastructure.public-broadband
definition: no = state law bars or materially restricts municipal/public broadband (bans, referendum requirements, feasibility or cost tests, unserved-area limits, bans on retail service) in force on 2026-01-01; yes = no such restriction, including states that repealed one (repeal date as operativeAt).
summarySource: ILSR/communitynetworks.org state preemption tracker (16 states after Minnesota's May 2024 repeal); Techdirt 11/07/2024 list; BroadbandNow 2023-2024 roadblocks reports.

US-AK.note: Not among the 16 states ILSR and BroadbandNow list as restricting municipal broadband (2024); no state-specific statute confirming the absence of a barrier was checked.

US-AL.note: Municipalities may provide service but face conditions, including a bar on using local tax revenue for network start-up costs.

US-AR.cite: Ark. Code Ann. § 23-17-409 (as amended by Act 764 of 2021)
US-AR.note: Act 764 of 2021 removed most of the prior ban on government-provided broadband; the exact effective date was not confirmed.

US-CO.note: SB23-183, signed in early May 2023, repealed the SB 05-152 referendum requirement; the exact effective date was not confirmed.

unknown.US-IA: Not on the ILSR 16-state list, but Iowa Code § 388.2 requires a referendum to establish a city utility, including telecommunications; could not verify whether trackers count this as a restriction (search budget exhausted).
unknown.US-DC: Not a state; no tracker classifies D.C., and D.C. law on selling retail broadband was not confirmed.

conflicts.readings: ILSR's 2024 list of 16 restricted states omits Iowa; Iowa Code § 388.2 nonetheless requires a referendum to create a city utility, which the definition counts as a restriction.
BroadbandNow has also counted up to 25 states with burdensome laws, and ILSR's earlier list had 19; the 2024 consensus list is 16. States outside the 16 were answered yes on the tracker list alone.
